lessons.title: The offside position
lessons.objective: You can spot an offside position at the moment of the pass.

payload.prompt: Tap the half of the pitch where a player can be in an offside position.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of a full pitch. Your team attacks toward the top goal. The halfway line splits the pitch into your own half at the bottom and the opponents' half at the top.

explanation.correct: Right. You can only be in an offside position in the opponents' half. Being level with the halfway line, or in your own half, is never offside.
explanation.incorrect: A player cannot be in an offside position in his own half of the pitch. Offside only applies in the half where you are attacking.
explanation.sayThisLine: You can't be offside in your own half.

payload.prompt: An attacker's shoulder is nearer goal than the second-last defender. In an offside position?

scene.alt: A striker's upper body is slightly ahead of the second-last defender and the ball is behind him at the moment the pass is played forward.

explanation.correct: Correct. Any part of the head, body or feet nearer the goal line puts the attacker in an offside position at the moment of the pass.
explanation.incorrect: Yes, if any part of the head, body or feet is nearer the opponent's goal line than both the ball and the second-last opponent at the moment of the pass, the attacker is in an offside position.
explanation.sayThisLine: His shoulder was just offside, that's enough.

payload.prompt: At which moment is an offside position judged?

options.text: The moment the ball is kicked
The moment the striker receives it
When the striker touches the ball inside the box

explanation.correct: Right. Offside position is judged at the moment the pass leaves the passer's foot, not when the attacker receives it.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is a snapshot taken when the ball is played. Where the attacker runs afterwards does not change whether he was in an offside position at that moment.

payload.prompt: Complete the offside rule.
payload.template: An attacker is in an offside position if any part of the {{parts}} is nearer the goal line than the {{opponents}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Head, body and feet count; arms do not. The second-last opponent includes the keeper.
explanation.incorrect: The rule applies to head, body and feet (not arms), and measures against the second-last opponent (the keeper plus one defender minimum).

lessons.title: Position is not an offence
lessons.objective: You can explain why standing offside is not always an offence.

payload.prompt: Attacker in offside position but doesn't touch the ball. Offence?

scene.alt: An attacker stands in an offside position, the ball is passed to a teammate in an onside position, and the onside player scores.

explanation.correct: No offence. Being in an offside position is not an offence by itself. Only if the player interferes with play, interferes with an opponent or gains an advantage does it become an offence.
explanation.incorrect: The rule is clear: an attacker can stand in an offside position all day. It becomes an offence only if they play the ball, interfere with an opponent or gain an advantage from the position.

payload.prompt: An attacker in an offside position stands in front of the keeper and blocks his view. Offence?

options.text: No, only if he touches the ball
Yes, he interferes with an opponent
No, the referee decides later

explanation.correct: Yes. Clearly obstructing an opponent's line of vision, so he cannot play the ball, is interfering with an opponent and makes the offside position an offence.
explanation.incorrect: An offside-position attacker can commit an offence without touching the ball. Clearly blocking the keeper's view or movement counts as interfering with an opponent.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: Offside position, but he never touched it so no offence.

payload.question: What is she saying?

options.text: You can be in an offside position without committing an offence
The attacker was not trying to score
The referee made a mistake calling it offside
Being offside only matters if you're involved

payload.translation: Standing in an offside position is only an offence if the player touches the ball, interferes with an opponent or gains an advantage from the position.

followUps.line: Can an offside player interfere without touching?
followUps.why: Tests deeper understanding of the rule.

followUps.line: How does gaining an advantage work?
followUps.why: Explores the third way the rule applies.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The distinction between position and offence trips up even experienced viewers; you are in good company.

payload.prompt: Complete the offence rule.
payload.template: An attacker in an offside position commits an offence only if he {{play}}, interferes with an opponent, or {{gain}} from being there.

explanation.correct: Right. Three ways to turn a position into an offence: play the ball, interfere with an opponent, or gain an advantage from being offside.
explanation.incorrect: Standing in an offside position is not enough. It becomes an offence if he plays the ball, interferes with an opponent, or gains an advantage, for example by playing a ball that rebounds off the post or a save.

lessons.title: Level is onside
lessons.objective: You can call level as onside and know which body parts count.

payload.prompt: Attacker level with the last defender at the moment of the pass. Onside?

scene.alt: A striker's feet are exactly in line with the last defender's feet when the pass is played forward.

explanation.correct: Yes. Level is onside. To be offside, the attacker must be nearer the goal line than the second-last opponent, so being level counts as onside.
explanation.incorrect: Level with the second-last opponent is onside. He has to be nearer the goal line, not just equal, to be in an offside position.

payload.prompt: Attacker's arm is ahead of the last defender. Offside position?

options.text: Yes, the arm counts
No, arms do not count for offside
Only if the arm is raised

explanation.correct: Right. For offside, only the head, body and feet count. Hands and arms, measured from the bottom of the armpit down, do not.
explanation.incorrect: Hands and arms never make a player offside. Only the head, body and feet are judged, so an arm stretched past the defender changes nothing.

payload.prompt: Attacker's knee is onside but toe is offside. Offside position?

scene.alt: An attacker's knee is level with the last defender, but the attacker's toe extends just past the defender's foot.

explanation.correct: Correct. Any part of the feet (including a toe) that is nearer the goal line than the second-last opponent puts the attacker in an offside position.
explanation.incorrect: If any part of the feet is ahead of the defender's feet, it's an offside position. The whole foot doesn't need to be past the line, just the toe.

payload.prompt: Complete the body parts rule.
payload.template: For offside, {{included}} count, but {{excluded}} do not.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Head, body and feet are judged. Hands and arms, from the bottom of the armpit down, are not.
explanation.incorrect: Hands and arms do not count for offside. Head, body and feet do, so a stretched-out arm never makes a player offside.

lessons.title: Read the line (sim)
lessons.objective: You can read the offside line at the moment of the pass under time pressure.

payload.prompt: When you read the line on a replay, which frame do you freeze?

options.text: The frame the ball leaves the passer's foot
The frame the attacker controls the ball
The frame the ball crosses the goal line

explanation.correct: Right. Offside position is judged at the moment the ball is played by the passer. Freeze that frame and compare the attacker with the second-last opponent.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is decided when the pass is played, not when the attacker receives it or when the ball reaches the goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: Freeze it when the ball leaves his foot.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Offside by a toenail. That's so harsh!

options.text: His toe was fractionally ahead of the second-last defender
A tiny margin decided the offside call
He was fouled in the box
The ball did not cross the line

payload.translation: The attacker was in an offside position by the smallest margin, so the goal or chance was ruled out even though it looked close to level.

followUps.line: Do you think they should change the rule?
followUps.why: Invites her opinion on the debate.

payload.prompt: He was offside when the pass left, then ran back onside before touching it. Offence?

scene.alt: A striker was in an offside position when the pass was played, then moved into an onside area before receiving the ball.

explanation.correct: Correct. The player's position at the moment of the pass is what counts, not where they are after receiving the ball. Once offside, a player cannot make themselves onside by running back.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is judged at the moment the pass is played, not when the receiver touches the ball. Movement after receiving it does not change the offside decision.

payload.prompt: Complete the timing rule.
payload.template: Offside is judged at the moment the {{action}} leaves the passer's foot, not when the receiver {{action2}}.

explanation.correct: Exactly. The timing is crucial: offside is decided by positions at the moment of the pass, not reception.
explanation.incorrect: Offside is a snapshot decision taken at the moment the pass leaves the passer's foot.

lessons.title: Deliberate play or deflection
lessons.objective: You can explain why a defender's deliberate touch resets offside and a deflection does not.

payload.prompt: A pass deflects off a defender's shin to an attacker who was offside. Still offside?

scene.alt: A pass is deflected off a defender's shin as he tries to block it. An attacker who was in an offside position when it was played receives the ball.

explanation.correct: Still offside. A deflection or accidental touch does not reset the offside line. Only a deliberate play by the defender does.
explanation.incorrect: A block or deflection is not the same as a deliberate play. If a defender doesn't deliberately play the ball, the offside line stays the same.

payload.prompt: Defender deliberately heads a loose ball back. Next attacker was offside. Onside now?

scene.alt: A defender jumps and deliberately heads a bouncing ball back toward his own goal. An attacker who was in an offside position receives the pass.

explanation.correct: Correct. A deliberate play by a defender, such as a header or a pass, means the attacker who receives the ball is not penalised for offside.
explanation.incorrect: When a defender deliberately plays the ball, the attacker receiving it is not judged offside from the earlier pass. A deflection or block is different.

payload.prompt: A keeper makes a save and the ball rebounds to an attacker who was offside on the shot. Offside?

options.text: Yes, a save is not a deliberate play
No, any touch by the keeper resets offside
Only if the keeper catches the ball

explanation.correct: Right. A save does not count as a deliberate play, so an attacker who was offside on the shot and gains from the rebound is penalised.
explanation.incorrect: Only a deliberate play by a defender resets offside. A goalkeeper's save is not counted as one, so the rebound can still be offside.
explanation.sayThisLine: A save does not reset offside.

payload.prompt: Complete the rule.
payload.template: A {{action}} play by a defender resets offside, but a {{action2}} does not.

explanation.correct: Right. The rule rewards defenders who actively play the ball; a deflection or accident does not reset the line.
explanation.incorrect: Only a deliberate play (an intentional control, pass or header) by a defender resets the offside line. Blocks and deflections do not.

lessons.title: How VAR works
lessons.objective: You can explain what VAR can and cannot review.

payload.prompt: VAR can review which of these?

options.text: A throw-in decision in midfield
Whether a goal should stand
A first yellow card
A goal-kick decision

explanation.correct: Right. VAR reviews goals, penalties, direct red cards and mistaken identity. From 2026/27 it can also look at clearly wrong second yellows and some corner decisions.
explanation.incorrect: VAR is limited to match-changing decisions: goals, penalties, direct red cards and mistaken identity, plus the new 2026/27 additions. Throw-ins, goal kicks and first yellows are not on the list.

payload.prompt: Match the VAR term to what it means.

pairs.definition: VAR reviews silently in the room, no interruption; only tells the ref if there is a clear error.
The referee walks to the monitor to look at replays and decides, or VAR advises and the ref chooses.
The error must be so evident that any official looking at a replay would see it immediately.

explanation.summary: A check is silent and quick, and a review sends the referee to the monitor. For judgment calls the error must be clear and obvious; factual calls like offside are simply measured.
explanation.sayThisLine: They went to the monitor, that's a review.

statement.speaker: Him
statement.text: VAR only steps in for a clear and obvious error.

options.text: Subjective calls are usually left with the referee
The mistake must be clear, not just debatable
VAR can rerun every decision
VAR reviews everything in slow motion

payload.translation: For judgment calls, VAR only interferes when the referee has made a clear mistake. Factual calls, such as whether a player was offside, are simply checked.

followUps.line: Was it clear or just close?
Do you think the referee should have gone to the screen?

payload.prompt: From 2026/27, VAR can review a clearly wrong second yellow card. True or false?

scene.alt: A player is sent off after a second yellow card that looked mistaken on replay.

explanation.correct: True. For 2026/27 the list of VAR reviews grows to include clearly incorrect second yellow cards leading to a red, alongside mistaken identity and some corner decisions.
explanation.incorrect: IFAB's 2026/27 changes extend VAR to clearly wrong second yellows, since they end up as a red card. A first yellow is still not reviewable.
explanation.sayThisLine: VAR can now look at a wrong second yellow.

lessons.title: Line, active play and VAR (sim)
lessons.objective: You can read the line and active play as in a VAR review.

payload.prompt: An attacker in an offside position just runs past the play without touching or blocking. Active play?

options.text: Yes, he is in an offside position
No, he neither played the ball nor affected an opponent
Yes, because the goal was scored

explanation.correct: Right. He is in an offside position but not in active play, because he did not play the ball, interfere with an opponent or gain an advantage. So there is no offence.
explanation.incorrect: Active play means touching the ball, interfering with an opponent or gaining an advantage. Simply being in an offside position while running past is not enough.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: They didn't draw those lines by hand, the system did it in seconds.

options.text: Semi-automated offside technology
Camera tracking that shows where the players were
A referee measuring with a tape
A replay of a foul

payload.translation: Semi-automated offside technology uses tracking cameras and the ball's data to place the offside line in seconds, so decisions come back quicker than hand-drawn lines.

followUps.line: Does it feel quicker than the old way?
followUps.why: Shows curiosity about how it works.
Invites her to tell the story.

payload.prompt: Complete the active-play rule.
payload.template: A player in an offside position is in active play if he {{play}}, {{interfere}}, or {{gain}} from that position.

explanation.correct: Exactly. Three routes: play the ball, interfere with an opponent, or gain an advantage.
explanation.incorrect: An offside attacker commits an offence if they play the ball, interfere with an opponent or gain an advantage.

lessons.title: The trap and the debates
lessons.objective: You can explain the offside trap and the arguments about the rule.

payload.prompt: How does an offside trap work?

options.text: The back line stays deep and compact
The entire back line steps up at the moment of the pass to catch attackers
One centre-back moves forward while others stay

explanation.correct: Correct. A coordinated offside trap means the entire back line steps up in unison at the instant the pass is played, hoping to leave attackers in an offside position.
explanation.incorrect: An offside trap requires perfect timing: all defenders move forward together the moment the pass leaves the passer, catching the attackers offside.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: That's the trap, the whole back line stepped up together.

payload.question: What is she describing?

options.text: A planned defensive move to catch offside
A foul by the back line
The defenders moving high up the pitch
A trap to catch an attacker fouling

payload.translation: The defensive line (all four or five defenders) moves up as one unit at the moment an opponent plays a pass, hoping to leave attackers in an offside position.

followUps.why: Tests understanding of the danger: if it fails, defenders are beaten.

followUps.line: When do teams use it most?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: The trap is a high-risk, high-reward tactic. One mistimed step and the attacker is one-on-one with the keeper.

payload.prompt: What is the 'daylight' offside proposal?

options.text: Offside only in daytime matches
An attacker is offside only if his whole body is clearly ahead
VAR must use natural light

explanation.correct: Right. Under the 'daylight' idea, an attacker would be offside only if there is clear space between his body and the last defender. It would stop toenail calls. It has been debated but not adopted.
explanation.incorrect: The 'daylight' offside proposal says an attacker is offside only if there is clear space (daylight) between him and the last defender. It has been debated but not adopted, and no offside change was approved for 2026/27.

payload.title: The offside goal
payload.setting: She is angry about a disallowed goal decided by SAOT.

exchanges.theirMessage: Offside by a toenail! They're checking every pixel with that technology.

replies.text: That toenail is in the rules though, even if it feels harsh.
replies.theirResponse: Maybe, but it changes the whole game.
replies.coachNote: Acknowledges her frustration while defending the rule.

replies.theirResponse: You just want your team to get away with it.

replies.text: Do you think they should adopt the daylight rule instead?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe. Less of these toenail calls.
replies.coachNote: Shows you understand the debate and respect both views.

payload.closingNote: She is frustrated by the precision of technology applied to a marginal rule. The daylight-rule proposal is one attempt to fix it.
